metadata.methods_description: Participants performed a visual search task on some scenes and an intentional memorization task on others while EEG and eye movements were recorded. A surprise recognition memory test with remember-know judgments followed. Behavioral data are provided separately for encoding (Encode_beh) and testing (Test_beh).

citation_details.title: What masking geometry works best for EEG foundation models?
citation_details.author: Pierre Guetschel, Bruno Aristimunha, Yassine El Ouahidi, Arnaud Delorme A, Thomas Moreau, Michael Tangermann
citation_details.abstract: EEG foundation models hold promise for scalable brain-signal decoding across clinical and cognitive neuroscience applications, yet their pre-training pipelines remain poorly understood. Among design choices, the masking strategy is particularly critical: it determines what the network must predict and from which context. Yet it has never been ablated in isolation, as each new model bundles a new masking strategy with a new backbone and objective. In this paper, we formalize the design choices for spatio-temporal masking strategies and train various models with a single pipeline under varying masking configurations across two SSL frameworks (MAE and JEPA). We then systematically evaluate the resulting 58 pre-trained models on the 12 datasets of OpenEEGBench under a linear probe. Both frameworks agree on an optimal masking configuration and on shared failure modes. Outside these, performance is robust: 11 MAE and 9 JEPA configurations are statistically indistinguishable from the best. We further identify a novel JEPA-specific failure mode, tagged bias-inflation collapse, invisible to standard detectors. With a well-chosen mask, our pipeline reaches REVE-level downstream performance at a fraction of REVE's pre-training compute.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

citation_details.title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
citation_details.author: Kuber Shahi, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme A
citation_details.abstract: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

citation_details.title: REVE: A Foundation Model for EEG - Adapting to Any Setup with Large-Scale Pretraining on 25,000 Subjects
citation_details.author: Yassine El Ouahidi, Jonathan Lys, Philipp Thölke, Nicolas Farrugia, Bastien Pasdeloup, Vincent Gripon, Karim Jerbi, Giulia Lioi
citation_details.abstract: Foundation models have transformed AI by reducing reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While successful in language and vision, their adoption in EEG has lagged due to the heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and electrode configurations. Existing EEG foundation models struggle to generalize across these variations, often restricting pretraining to a single setup, resulting in suboptimal performance, in particular under linear probing. We present REVE (Representation for EEG with Versatile Embeddings), a pretrained model explicitly designed to generalize across diverse EEG signals. REVE introduces a novel 4D positional encoding scheme that enables it to process signals of arbitrary length and electrode arrangement. Using a masked autoencoding objective, we pretrain REVE on over 60,000 hours of EEG data from 92 datasets spanning 25,000 subjects, representing the largest EEG pretraining effort to date. REVE achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 downstream EEG tasks, including motor imagery classification, seizure detection, sleep staging, cognitive load estimation, and emotion recognition. With little to no fine-tuning, it demonstrates strong generalization, and nuanced spatio-temporal modeling. We release code, pretrained weights, and tutorials to support standardized EEG research and accelerate progress in clinical neuroscience.

citation_details.title: Incidental encoding of objects during search is stronger than intentional memorization due to increased recollection rather than familiarity
citation_details.author: Melissa L.‐H. Võ, Dejan Draschkow, Jason Helbing
citation_details.abstract: Repository for "Incidental encoding of objects during search is stronger than intentional memorization due to increased recollection rather than familiarity" (Helbing, Draschkow, & Võ, 2025, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.a.80). Contains data analysis resources (preprocessed data and analysis script, EEG and ROC preprocessing scripts) and experimental materials (script implemented to run the experiment, participant instructions, stimuli). Raw EEG, eye tracking, and behavioral data are stored in an OpenNeuro repository at https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds005189.
